items.title: ‘Like an invisible stealth tax’: ways to shield your cash from UK inflation
items.author: Rupert Jones
items.content:
With living costs set to rise higher in 2027, here’s how you can help your savings and pension keep up with soaring prices

But inflation also acts as an invisible stealth tax on savings cash, silently taking a bite out of many people’s nest-eggs. When it is running high, the odds are that your savings are being eroded.

items.lbText:
With living costs set to rise higher in 2027, here’s how you can help your savings and pension keep up with soaring prices

F or many of us, it is when we go to the supermarket that we really notice the impact of inflation. The trolley-load of groceries that used to cost £80 has broken the £100 barrier , and some of the packets look smaller than they were.

But inflation also acts as an invisible stealth tax on savings cash, silently taking a bite out of many people’s nest-eggs. When it is running high, the odds are that your savings are being eroded.

UK inflation rose to 3.6% in October and the Bank of England expects it to rise even further, to about 5% by mid-2027 , as higher energy prices continue to push up costs and bills.

If your savings account interest rate is lower than the inflation rate, you are losing money in real terms, even if the balance in your account is growing.

It is much easier to beat inflation if you do not pay tax on the savings interest you earn. So if you are a non-taxpayer, or the money is in an Isa, any interest rate over 3.6% is inflation-beating.

If you do pay tax on the interest, you will need to earn a rate of interest that is a fair bit higher than inflation for your returns to outpace the rising cost of living.

Just to match 3.6% inflation, a basic-rate taxpayer would currently need to earn 4.5%, while a higher-rate taxpayer would need to earn 6%.

This is not about a few pence or even a couple of pounds. Based on current inflation and a £10,000 savings balance, choosing a one-year fixed-rate savings bond paying 5.21% (one of the top rates available this week) compared with an account paying 2% could leave a saver £321 better off over one year.

Lots of people will remember index-linked savings certificates, which were offered by National Savings and Investments (NS&I). They guaranteed that your investment would “grow in spending power each year, whatever happens to the cost of living”, but they are no longer available, though people can renew maturing certificates.

No other provider offers anything similar, so you need to get the best rate on savings that you can. The good news is that the financial data firm Moneyfacts says there are 1,649 available savings accounts that pay more than the 3.6% you need to match inflation if there is no tax to pay.

That includes 879 fixed-rate savings bonds, which typically involve you having to tie up your money for between six months and five years. At the time of writing, best-buy rates on these ranged from 4.67% on a six-month bond from GB Bank to 5.37% on a five-year bond from StreamBank.

That total also includes 130 easy access accounts. Top-paying providers include Chase and Cahoot, which were this week paying 4.75% (which includes an interest bonus for 12 months) and 4.52% respectively.

Meanwhile, more than 400 fixed-rate cash Isas pay more than 3.6%. This week, top payers included UBL UK offering 5.3% and Shawbrook Bank with 5.27%, though to get those rates you would need to tie your cash up for five years. Best-buy easy access cash Isas include those offered by the Chip and Moneybox apps, which pay an initial 4.87% and 4.86% respectively.

In the example above, based on inflation at 3.6% and £10,000 saved for one year, a one-year fixed-rate savings bond paying 5.21% would return a £521 interest payment at the end of the term. However, the real return after inflation would be £161, says Moneyfacts.

If the same sum was in an account paying 2%, while the saver would get £200 interest after a year, their real return after inflation would be negative. They would be £160 worse off in real terms.

Caitlyn Eastell at Moneyfacts says that with inflation forecast to continue going up, “it’s crucial that savers secure the most competitive rates to ensure their money isn’t losing its spending power”.

There are now more than 250 accounts that pay interest of 5% or more, which is “a real win for savers”, though it is increasingly important to make use of tax-efficient options such as cash Isas, she adds..

Although falling out of favour among retirees, an annuity is a product that turns an individual’s pension pot into a regular guaranteed income for the rest of their life, or for a fixed term . You pay a life insurer a lump sum, and in exchange it guarantees you a regular payout.

There are various types. Level annuities are the most popular – these pay the same income each year. But if you want to avoid inflation taking a bite out of your spending power over time, escalating annuities provide an income that goes up every year.

You can choose between an annual increase at a set rate, such as 3% or 5%, or one that is index-linked, which means it rises in line with inflation.

Usually the latter type is linked to the retail prices index rather than the consumer price index, even though RPI is considered by many to be a discredited measure. RPI inflation is usually higher than CPI inflation: in October it was 4.2%.

If you opt for an annuity linked to inflation, or a set annual increase, your starting income will be a lot lower than if you go for a level annuity – which is one reason why the latter are so popular.

Earlier this month, a 65-year-old non-smoker who uses a £100,000 pension pot to buy a single-life annuity that rises in line with RPI and is guaranteed to pay out for a minimum of five years could get an initial annual income of just over £5,600. But if they went for a no-frills single-life level annuity, they would get just over £8,200 a year for the rest of their life.

When the UK government needs to borrow money, it can issue a bond ; these are often called gilts. The government pays interest on them, known as coupon payments, and it repays the initial bond value, known as the principal, to the investor at the end of the term.…

items.lbText:
German company faced 65,000 claims from people who said they developed cancer after using weedkiller

A Missouri judge on Friday approved Bayer ’s $7.25bn settlement of lawsuits ⁠alleging that its weedkiller ​Roundup causes cancer, potentially resolving litigation that has weighed on the German company for close to a decade.

Judge Timothy Boyer of a state court in St Louis ⁠found the settlement “fair, reasonable and adequate”.

He overruled objections that payouts to individual cancer victims would be too low because claimants who previously settled were paid more.

The judge also said delaying payouts could ⁠force victims, including those whose cancer is terminal, to wait “an indeterminate number of years” to be paid.

Bayer had faced approximately ​65,000 claims in US state and federal courts from ‌people who said they developed cancer ‌after using Roundup at home or on the job.

The settlement announced in February aimed to resolve nearly all current ‌and future Roundup claims in the US.

“The court’s final approval is a decisive milestone in the company’s strategy to mitigate the risks of both pending and future Roundup litigation,” Bayer’s CEO, Bill Anderson, said in a statement.

Bayer has faced extensive litigation over Roundup, and had seen its share price fall 46% since it bought Monsanto , which produces the weedkiller, for $63bn in 2018.

The company settled much of the Roundup litigation for $10.9bn in 2020, ‌but was unable to win court approval of a $1.25bn settlement to resolve future Roundup claims.

Bayer has long maintained that Roundup and its active ingredient glyphosate were safe, and that decades ​of studies had shown that glyphosate did not cause cancer.

The settlement was approved five months after the US supreme court overturned a $1.25m jury award for a Missouri man, John Durnell, who blamed years of exposure to glyphosate in Roundup for his non-Hodgkin lymphoma.

In a 7-2 decision, the court agreed with Bayer that a federal law regulating pesticides barred failure-to-warn claims brought under ⁠state law, undercutting a central pillar of many lawsuits.

Christopher Seeger, a lawyer for ​many of the plaintiffs, said the Durnell ​decision narrowed the ability of Roundup victims ​to pursue claims in court.

“We look forward to getting this relief into the hands of all ​Roundup victims as quickly ‌as possible,” he ​said in a statement.

Lawyers for ​some of the Roundup victims who objected to the settlement did not immediately respond to requests for comment.

The settlement excludes some lawsuits that remain pending in federal court. Bayer has said that about 200 of those cases were still being litigated, and that the supreme court decision gave it strong defenses.

items.title: GTA 6 sales hit $3.8bn in a single day - the biggest entertainment launch in history
items.content: <article>The mammoth figure surpasses every video game launch and single-day film box office record.</article>
items.lbText:
Grand Theft Auto 6 is estimated to have become the biggest entertainment launch in history following the blockbuster video game's debut on Thursday , after a 13-year wait.

The highly anticipated open-world action-adventure saw pre-orders and first day sales total more than 24.5 million units, raking in about $2.36bn (£1.8bn), according to analytics platform Sensor Tower.

In comparison, this year's highest grossing movie so far, Spider-Man: Brand New Day, made $2.5bn over its entire run in cinemas .

GTA 6's maker Rockstar and parent company Take-Two have not released details of the game's sales but said demand has been "unprecedented". The BBC has contacted both the firms for comment.

The game is the latest instalment in Rockstar's nearly three decade old crime simulator franchise, which has become one of the most popular games in history .

At its core, the series is a satirical take on the American dream, putting players in the shoes of career criminals in Leonida, the game's Florida-inspired state.

The latest release follows new characters Lucia and her partner Jason, a pair of small-time criminals.

GTA 6 is estimated to have cost more than $1bn to develop , which would make it the most expensive video game in history.

Sensor Tower said GTA 6 will be so popular that it will reduce the time gamers spend on other single-player titles by 10%.

The research firm said its estimates are based on email receipts data and other statistical sources that track millions of people daily. They also track public profiles across major gaming platforms like PlayStation and Xbox, where GTA 6 is available.

Around three quarters of the game's sales have been for the PlayStation 5 and the balance on Xbox, Sensor Tower said.

Niko Partners, a gaming market research firm, said it expects GTA 6 to make more than $3bn in sales worldwide this year.

That figure would rank GTA 6 among the highest-grossing entertainment releases ever, but it would still have some way to go to catch 1939's Gone with the Wind , which has made an estimated $4.5bn, adjusted for inflation.

Rockstar is expected to make even more money from GTA 6 over the coming years.

The New York-based studio has yet to announce when the game will be released for PCs or given a date for its multiplayer expansion, which will allow players to interact and go on missions with others over the internet.

If 2013's GTA 5 is any guide, multiplayer will add dozens more hours of gameplay and bring in even more revenue for Rockstar as players spend real money on in-game property, cars and other perks.

Anticipation for the blockbuster title has grown through repeated delays, following a 13-year wait.

GTA 6 has been hailed by some reviewers as one of the most impressive gaming experiences ever. Entertainment media site IGN described it as an "uncompromisingly engineered" masterpiece.

The release of GTA 6 at midnight on Thursday across various time zones saw many gamers stay up through the night, while some took the following day off to play.

Its launch broke Virgin Media O2's evening traffic record as people rushed to install GTA 6's huge 212GB file on consoles.

The game's graphic content has resulted in censorship in Japan and, like earlier GTA releases, is not approved for sale in mainland China.

items.title: Tech stock sell-off drags markets down as Anthropic shares slide
items.content: <article>Pressures weighed on US markets, with the S&P 500 and the Dow Jones Industrial Average pushed into correction territory.</article>
items.lbText:
Anthropic's shares have dropped back towards their initial price after a soaring first day on the stock market, as a wider tech sell-off deepens.

The fall in tech stocks continued to weigh on markets, with the S&P 500 down more than 2% and the Dow Jones Industrial Average down 0.7% by lunchtime.

Both US indexes touched correction territory, a point where they are trading at 10% or more down from a recent high.

The tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite Index also fell more than 3.4% by the middle of trading on Friday.

Despite a positive first day of trading, Anthropic's shares fell on Friday, dropping more than 12% to about $85 by lunchtime, close to its initial public offering (IPO) price of $83.

The artificial intelligence (AI) company's introduction to the Nasdaq stock exchange on Thursday was a crucial test for the industry and was largely seen as a success, with trading starting at $111.50.

The maker of the Claude chatbot raised a record $81bn in its initial public offering (IPO), but its share price moved significantly in the first day of trading.

The shares peaked at $115 on Thursday, before easing to end the day up 17% at $97.17.

Analysts said volatility was to be expected in the first days or even weeks of Anthropic's trading, as the company was the first frontier AI firm to go public so had no direct peers.

Some have also noted the similarities with Elon Musk's SpaceX, which at the time of its debut in June was the largest IPO on record. Shares in the rocket and AI company experienced large swings in its first few weeks of trading.

Ed Moya, a strategist at market intelligence firm AlphaSense, said Anthropic's blockbuster IPO did not appear to have restored confidence in the broader AI market.

While AI demand was still very strong, Moya told the BBC that investors were trying to answer the question of how much were they willing to pay for that growth.

"As we've gone through the past past few weeks, it seems that there's been more risks that have surfaced," he said.

"Right now you're starting to see Wall Street is trying to shift from rewarding growth at any price, to demanding stronger cash flow and a clearer path to profitability."

Shares in some of the largest US tech companies also fell.

Nvidia and SpaceX were both down more than 6%, while Tesla shares fell more than 3% and Meta was down 3.4%.

Apple, Amazon and Microsoft experienced smaller falls, while Alphabet was up by 1.2%.

Europe's main stock markets - which contain fewer tech stocks - were also trading lower. Germany's Dax index fell 2% and the UK's FTSE 100 was down 0.5%.

Earlier on Friday, tech-heavy Asian markets saw steep falls.

South Korea's Kospi and Japan's Nikkei 225 indexes closed down about 5%, with shares in memory chip makers Sk Hynix, Kioxia and Tokyo Electron, and other tech firms such as Samsung Electronics, seeing losses.

Taiwan's stock market dropped about 6% on Friday, taking the weekly fall to more than 17% and what was reported to be its biggest weekly fall since 1990.

items.title: Trump threatens ban on US firms building AI data centres overseas
items.content: <article>The US president provided little detail on the potential policy, saying others in his team were hearing about it for the first time.</article>
items.lbText:
Donald Trump has said he will ban US companies from building AI data centres overseas, threatening a "tremendous tax" for tech firms who do so.

"We're going to keep it all in this country," the US president said, while providing little detail on the potential policy he said others in his cabinet were hearing about for the first time.

Data centres were a central issue in the midterm elections earlier in November, with many Democratic candidates promising tougher regulation on their construction.

Tech giants including Meta and Google have entered agreements to build data centres overseas. It remains unclear how such a policy would be enforced if it was brought in.

"We're not going to allow our companies to build data centres outside of our country," Trump told reporters in a press briefing following his return from his trip to Asia.

"Because China will take all of them, and we're not allowing that to happen."

But whether that idea will become policy remains unclear.

"I don't know if that's a breaking story, but I haven't even said that to my people. But I'm telling them now, they're here," he said.

Trump floated the policy after saying the US was leading on data centre construction, and he would not allow China to beat the US when it came to AI - which he calls super intelligence, or SI.

It also follows an announcement earlier this week that would restrict the export of advanced computer chips and who can access the computing power provided by them.

Washington on Monday announced firms would require a licence to buy advanced chips, so US officials can monitor whether they are being used to serve Chinese companies or they are being smuggled into China.

The move will impact South East Asian countries that have invested heavily in data centres, as Chinese companies seek to rent computing power from overseas.

Why Canada is embracing AI data centres while the US pushes back

Data centres are crucial to the AI boom. The vast warehouse-style buildings house the advanced computer chips and servers that are needed to run AI programmes such as Claude and ChatGPT.

As of April there were about 3,000 data centres across the US, with another 1,500 in various stages of approval and construction, according to the Pew Research Centre.

Many of them are built in rural areas, and concerns about issues including noise pollution and energy consumption helped drive Democratic candidates promising tougher rules on data centre construction to wins on 3 November.

"You ought to take advantage of the data centres. Make them pay you, make them pay your community, but take advantage don't shut them off," Trump said.

"We have a lot of places that want them badly, and they're great places. They have energy and they have everything. They're tremendous assets."

Large tech firms - often called AI hyperscalers due to the size of their investments in AI - have also been branching out, and Canada has made moves to step in to offer itself as an alternative location for these sites, with less local pushback against projects so far.

Meta has already broken ground on a data centre , external in the province of Alberta, and Anthropic has signed a long-term agreement to lease a proposed data centre in Nova Scotia.

The BBC has reached out to Meta for comment on Trump's remarks.

In September Google announced a €13bn ($15bn: £11bn) investment in AI infrastructure in Finland, which included funding for three data centres.

Last month, building work for two of those centres was halted due to concerns over the clearance of more than 300 hectares of forest.

Trump called out the build in Finland specifically, saying his administration was "not allowing that to happen".

items.title: What exactly is in the deal between the UK and the EU?
items.author: Jennifer Rankin and Alexandra Topping
items.content:
The two sides have come to agreements on food and drink, emissions trading and the youth exchange scheme

After months of on-off negotiations, leaks and late nights, the EU and UK have agreed a 12-page statement setting out the next steps in their relationship. What exactly have they agreed?

Continue reading...
items.lbText:
The two sides have come to agreements on food and drink, emissions trading and the youth exchange scheme

Burnham has agreed EU reset deal with tuition fees issue unresolved, says No 10

After months of on-off negotiations, leaks and late nights, the EU and UK have agreed a 12-page statement setting out the next steps in their relationship. What exactly have they agreed?

The UK agreed to work closely with the EU’s “Channel action plan”, which aims to crack down on smugglers who organise small boat crossings. The agreement will see law enforcement intelligence sharing between the UK and the EU, working closer with agencies such as Europol and the European border agency Frontex, and improved maritime surveillance from French authorities.

The agreement promises “a new structured dialogue” on migration, with both sides pledging to disrupt smuggling networks, strengthening border management in the Channel to stop small boat crossings, and work more closely with countries along migration routes. Both sides will require “shared financial commitments” given the “shared nature” of the challenges, according to the agreement.

Von der Leyen said Britain and the bloc would work together along the entire migration route and to prevent dangerous Channel crossings, which she argued would also save lives. Burnham also expressed interest in the plans of five EU member states to negotiate an offshore “returns hub” with Rwanda for people with no right to stay in the EU.

In a significant win for the UK, the EU has agreed to “explore further mutually beneficial solutions” on touring artists.

This does not sound like much. But the Labour government has spent more than two years making the case for easier access to the EU for travelling artists, musicians and performers, who face cumbersome work permits and complex rules for tour vehicles and equipment. Government-commissioned research suggests Brexit touring barriers have cost the UK sector £208m and nearly 2,500 jobs.

The EU has long refused to open discussions, so an agreement to talk is a breakthrough. Nonetheless it might not seem much to artists snared in red tape when working on the continent. The Musicians Union general secretary, Naomi Pohl, said members would be “extremely disappointed”, adding that she hoped “resolving this issue will be a priority”.

The document details plans to launch a new bilateral agreement – the EU-UK digital partnership – early next year. It will aim to increase cooperation on technology issues such as AI, connectivity, critical technologies, digital wallets and online safety with both parties maintaining “regulatory autonomy”.

In a potential advance for the UK, the EU appears ready to expand talks on the mutual recognition of professional qualifications, beyond existing negotiations on architects.

The statement welcomes “significant progress” on mutual recognition of professional qualifications for architects under the trade and cooperation agreement (TCA), and both sides agreed to “explore” arrangements in other professions.

items.title: The Guardian view on Britain and Europe: Burnham’s reset cannot be the final destination | Editorial
items.author: Editorial
items.content:
It’s welcome news that Labour has reopened doors that the Conservatives slammed shut. But the fundamental dilemma over European integration remains

Andy Burnham on Friday announced a long-awaited deal to ease some of Brexit’s barriers. But EU sources say the agreements, or at least some of them, won’t take effect until Britain has resolved a dispute over its demand for European students to pay the same university tuition fees as British ones. The prime minister had hoped to turn the page on Brexit’s endless haggling. Instead, he was reminded that closer ties come at a price. This does not negate his achievement. The deals ease trade barriers on food, shield British exporters from EU carbon tariffs and let up to 100,000 young people on each side live and work across the Channel for three years. But Mr Burnham cannot claim an unqualified diplomatic victory.

Clearly, such an advance would have been unimaginable under the Conservatives or Reform. The Tories say they will rip up the agreements, though that stance carries the risk of alienating voters lost to the Liberal Democrats in 2024. Nigel Farage admits that Brexit was botched. But he wants greater divergence from, rather than increased closeness to, Europe. Both rightwing parties face a dilemma: how to oppose the better relationship when even Mr Farage acknowledges its benefits?

News of vulnerability comes after retailers in at least seven European countries hit by cyber-attacks

A secret government cybersecurity operation recently warded off the risk of a cyber-attack on fridges and freezers in UK supermarkets, warehouses, restaurants, petrol stations and stadiums, it has emerged.

An attack would have been similar to those that have caused many millions of euros of damage in continental Europe in recent months. But, while many retailers have now been protected, researchers warned that many more could still be vulnerable.

News of the operation led by Whitehall and the National Cyber Security Centre, first reported by the BBC, follows a cyberattack this month of supermarket chains in at least seven European countries.

Another wave of attacks also affected hundreds of retailers across France in October in an act of “unprecedented scale and unprecedented aggression” for which Paris has publicly blamed Iran . The Pentagon is also investigating a suspected hack after a series of fridge malfunctions hit at least six US military bases in August.

Experts told the Guardian that if the vulnerability in UK-based devices had been discovered and exploited before a fix was found, the consequences would have been serious.

“This incident should serve as a wake-up call for the entire refrigeration industry,” said Garry Turner-Smith of Omega Solutions, a refrigeration consultancy firm whose employee, Neil McCourt, found the vulnerability in devices manufactured by Resource Data Management (RDM).

He said: “Had these weaknesses been discovered and exploited by someone with malicious intentions, they could have gained full control of vulnerable RDM data managers and used that access to interfere with refrigeration systems across multiple sites. This raises the prospect of attacks similar to those seen in Europe.”

After Omega was alerted to the weakness, the firm called in the cybersecurity consultants Pen Test Partners to investigate. Both firms then raised their concerns with the manufacturer, RDM.

Ken Munro, Pen Test Partners’ managing partner, said: “We determined that there was an urgent requirement to alert supermarkets and the food supply chain to the issue and fix. “However, we also had to work quietly to avoid alerting less ethical hackers and nation states of the likes of Iran, who are active in this space.”

Munro was attending a retail industry cyber event the day the vulnerabilities were found, enabling him to meet National Cyber Security Centre representatives in person to share the intelligence.

That triggered a series of briefing calls between retailers and officials from the National Cyber Security Centre, the Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs and the Food Standards Agency, among others, Munro said.

He added that Pen Test Partners had also tried to alert the owners of exposed devices. “Some controllers were easy to identify and thus contact the owners, but many thousands at small stores are still exposed,” he said.

“The vulnerability is not easy to find for a number of reasons, but once the method is known, it’s easy to recreate. We have not published that method, so there is still time for small operators to take their controllers off the public internet and/or apply the updated firmware.”

A National Cyber Security Centre spokesperson said it had “shared important insight and security advice to ensure that organisations understood potential risks to their networks, and were taking the appropriate measures to mitigate them”.

RDM did not respond to a request for comment. Its chief executive, Ged Evans, told the BBC the vulnerability was “identified in a test environment” that “went beyond” what such exercises usually involved as it “included dismantling our hardware”.

Evans saidd: “In any event we have acted at pace to address this issue and have already deployed first patch releases and have been in proactive contact with our customers to flag any issues and recommend mitigatory steps.”

items.title: UK to explore even closer ties with EU after agreeing deal, says Burnham
items.content: <article>The UK-EU deal agreed on Friday covers British food exports, emissions trading and a youth experience scheme.</article>
items.lbText:
Andy Burnham said the UK will discuss possible options for even closer ties with the EU, after agreeing a deal covering British food exports, emissions trading and a youth experience scheme.

The prime minister said it was a "good day" for Britain and Europe, adding the Treasury believes the deal could boost the UK economy by up to £17bn a year.

European Council President António Costa said the EU remains "open to have the closest possible relationship" with the UK.

Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch said the deal "isn't fair" - and Reform's Nigel Farage called it a "betrayal of the British people".

Legislation to implement the deal is expected to be introduced in the UK Parliament next week.

Burnham arrived in Brussels to finalise the latest stage of the government's post-Brexit "reset" of relations with the EU, which originally began under former prime minister Sir Keir Starmer.

The agreements announced on Friday included scrapping most of the checks on British food exports, in return for the UK following some EU regulations, from 2028.

The UK government believes the changes will cut costs for businesses and could bring prices down for shoppers, while critics argue the change will make the UK a "rule taker" from Brussels rather than a rule maker.

The new youth experience scheme will allow up to 100,000 18 to 31 year olds from the EU to travel, work and study in the UK for up to three years. The same number of young Britons will be allowed into Europe.

The two sides want to ensure that opportunities under the annual scheme will be available to young people by no later than January 2030.

A further six months is available to discuss a deal on tuition fees, which could prove to be a potential stumbling block.

There have been calls from the European side for fees to be reduced for EU students at British universities. The joint statement says any agreement would also be for UK students in the EU.

Burnham gets his first taste of EU dealmaking and seems hungry for more

What is the EU-UK youth experience scheme and when will it start?

Faisal Islam: This cost-cutting UK-EU deal doesn't mean lower prices will follow

European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said she is "confident" a solution will be found, with Burnham adding: "Me too."

On immigration, the UK and EU have committed to working closely to tackle migrant smuggling and human trafficking. They also expect their law enforcement agencies to share more data.

Burnham said "significant progress" has been made to help "disrupt the gangs who are making those dangerous crossings across the English Channel".

The UK-EU statement also said talks on linking the EU and UK emissions trading systems have concluded and they aim to apply the agreement from 2028.

Burnham argued that polling suggests the UK public "want closer ties" with the EU and the deal "delivers that".

He added: "Beyond that we do need to consider what is the right long-term relationship. Incremental steps only take us so far."

The prime minister said his government will publish a 10-year plan next month, adding it will set out its ambitions for reindustrialisation, growth in "all parts of Britain" and opportunities for young people.

Burnham said these ambitions are "connected to our long-term relationship with our nearest partner".

He said over the coming months before the next UK-EU summit both sides will "seek to conduct an informal brainstorming process" to look at what those options are.

Burnham added: "What we are announcing today is probably the limit of what we can achieve in this Parliament, given what needs to be done to implement it.

"But we want to inform the Parliament after this one, so that decisions can be taken about that long-term relationship."

Labour's 2024 general election manifesto pledged there would be "no return to the single market, the customs union, or freedom of movement", and Burnham has committed to this.

The prime minister said the "British people will be the boss of what happens next", with the next election needing to be held by August 2029.

Von der Leyen, who said the summit was a "turning point" for the EU-UK relationship, said "we are open for brainstorming".

Badenoch said the deal was not fair because UK farmers would now have to follow rules made by Brussels and more young people will come to the UK to "compete with our young people who are struggling to get jobs".

Badenoch was also asked about the Treasury's analysis, which Burnham said suggested the deal "will add up to 0.5%" to UK gross domestic product and he described it as a "£17bn boost to the British economy".

She claimed Burnham has "plucked that figure out of the air" and "the only modelling I've seen that even talks about that figure says it's actually 0.0%".

Farage said Friday was a "very good day for the EU", adding: "A good day to try and humiliate the one member state that actually had the courage to say, 'We don't need to be part of you, we can govern our own country'."

In a social media post, Farage, who was a leading figure in the 2016 campaign to get Britain out of the EU, added: "Like every prime minister before him, Burnham is a total fraud. Only Reform will stop the endless betrayal of the British people."

Liberal Democrat leader Sir Ed Davey said there needed to be more than "tweaks" to the UK's relationship to the EU.

"A youth mobility scheme is a big step forward, but it's nowhere near enough. We need a whole new deal that actually works for Britain, and fast."

items.title: Faisal Islam: This cost-cutting UK-EU deal doesn't mean lower prices will follow
items.content: <article>The trade deal is unlikely lower food prices for shoppers, but should boost the economy more than other post-Brexit agreements.</article>
items.lbText:
The prime minister made a lot of the UK's new deal with the EU cutting costs for business and consumers during tough times.

In another world, Andy Burnham would have loved for the nation's supermarkets to clearly announce that they could cut food prices as a result of this latest agreement on food exports.

And while grocers have very much welcomed Friday's announcement, they have notably not committed to price cuts as a direct result of this move.

The managing director of M&S, Alex Freudmann, called the deal a "major step forward", saying it would remove bureaucracy. Tesco chief executive Ken Murphy added it was "good news for British farmers and producers".

Freudmann highlighted some of hoops that were hurting UK-EU trade, using the example that "getting our spaghetti Bolognese from Lincolnshire onto a shelf in Dublin takes hundreds of extra miles, mountains of paperwork, a vet's signature and even the Latin name of a cow".

Such measures will no longer need to be taken once this deal kicks in. Good news for business exports then, but will that lead to lower shopping bills here in the UK?

This deal will matter for food exporters - it may not have a clear visible impact at the checkout.

Privately, industry insiders say there are too many moving parts in the world economy, especially given the energy price shock resulting from war in the Middle East.

It is more a hope than will at this stage. The industry and government hope that the reduction in costs for food producers and sellers will be passed on to customers.

This is not the first time Labour has sought to reduce the weekly shop costs. Sir Keir Starmer's administration floated the idea that supermarkets might even offer some form of branded discounts, a suggestion that was met with collective bemusement by those in the industry.

However, there will be less paperwork, checks and red tape on food imports too, but they were already lightly enforced.

No longer will hundreds of pages of documents be required. No longer will perishable goods lose valuable hours or days at border checks. No longer will the incorrect colour of ink or Latin name for a meat disallow a shipment of British exports.

Some, though not all of the 24% hit since 2019 to the real value of agrifood exports, could be regained by a bonfire of this red tape.

In particular, smaller exporters of food will be able to return to the large EU market.

But the extra benefit here is unclear, and there could be extra checks and costs required instead on non-EU food imports.

The government's own assessment is that the economy will gain £5bn through this, or 0.14% by 2040.

Critics point out that this benefit does not include the quid pro quo - having to align with EU laws. Farmers have pointed to compliance with pesticides and fungicide regulation.

The classic example of the benefits of post-Brexit autonomy has been the development of precision-bred foodstuffs, such as Vitamin D-enhanced tomatoes.

The producer of this technology has, however, backed the deal after the government negotiated an "exception period" for ongoing UK sale.

Professor Cristobal Uauy of the John Innes Centre said that "aligning with the EU market will bring our science to a greater number of people".

Bringing all the agreements on food, emissions and the youth experience together, the economy is forecast to get an overall boost of 0.5%, or £17bn a year.

A modest boost, but high by the standards of past post-Brexit trade deals, for example, with Australia, India or Japan and the Gulf and the trans-pacific deal.

This UK-EU pact actually matches all of those agreements combined for expected growth measured by the Treasury's own assessments.

The biggest single boost to the overall economy would come from more European young workers. However, the economy benefit of this part of the deal per person reduces to zero, according to the government's own calculations.

Burham also said he hoped a planned electricity deal with the EU would cut bills, but that has not been done yet, and requires a contribution into the bloc's budget for poorer regions.

The electricity deal could help lower bills, but that contains a clear trade-off.

There are still some details to be revealed in the full legal texts of these documents.

The bigger point is whether this logic of gaining free-flowing access for food, in exchange for giving up regulatory freedom, will now apply elsewhere.

Is food now a blueprint for future negotiations? It had been the Starmer-Rachel Reeves strategy to spread this model to other sectors such as cars, and chemicals.

The big takeaway from today was that both the PM and his counterparts publicly acknowledged the end of the incremental piecemeal approach to aligning with the single market.

The question is whether the PM thinks what goes for food applies across the whole economy. Most economists predict that could lead to much bigger economic gains, but it will also be a much bigger constitutional battle.

items.title: Airbnb's divisive new house rules come into force
items.content: <article>New rules on what Airbnb hosts can reasonably ask guests to do could mean fewer chores but higher costs for customers.</article>
items.lbText:
New rules on what Airbnb hosts can reasonably ask guests to do have come into force.

Hosts should now not normally ask guests to wash up, for example, but can appeal to Airbnb if they have a compelling reason.

Some guests have found lists of house rules laborious to complete, with one telling the BBC "it was not relaxing at all".

But some hosts have said that the costs of paying for extra cleaning may have to be passed on to customers.

The new Airbnb rules, announced last month , allow hosts to choose from seven standard house rules, which include determining how many people can stay overnight, and whether or not pets or smoking are allowed.

Hosts can then set additional rules, but guests shouldn't be asked to do the washing up, remove sheets from beds, take rubbish out or avoid using utilities.

Airbnb has begun reviewing listings and will be sending emails to hosts , external "who need to take action" it said.

Hosts can appeal to Airbnb to argue an additional house rule is necessary, and ask Airbnb to approve it.

If the house rule is not approved and the host keeps it anyway, Airbnb will flag this to guests on the host's listing page with a message such as "includes cleaning tasks".

Airbnb said chores can make customers hesitate about booking through the platform, arguing that making house rules "clearer" would increase the number of clients.

But some hosts have said they may have to pass the extra cleaning costs on to guests.

Lisa Clewes, who runs a Welsh holiday let, told the BBC she was "horrified" at the state her guests left the house after a dinner party.

There were broken glasses, drinks cans on the floor, pans full of food on the table and fish guts left in the garden.

Clewes said it typically takes cleaners four hours to turn around her three-bedroom property.

She said guests leaving more mess could mean hiring extra cleaners and increasing costs – expenses that may ultimately be passed on to her customers.

The changes have come as a relief to guests like Jessica Newhook, who says she has been faced with lengthy checkout lists, often on top of hefty cleaning fees.

She booked an Airbnb in Florida for a family reunion of 11 guests and says they had to "leave the property move-in ready for the cleaners", despite paying a $250 (£187) cleaning fee.

"We had rules about everything and it was not relaxing at all," she said.

The new rules have added to growing frustration among owners following increases in Airbnb's commission rates last year.

Many are investing in their own websites and social media to attract direct bookings and avoid platform fees.

Not all hosts are concerned about the changes, however.

Matt Porsz, who hosts and manages other Airbnb properties full-time, told the BBC previously the review system encourages both hosts and guests to behave reasonably.

items.lbText:
Three Choirs unveils First Release white wine after long, hot summer led to earliest harvest start in 50 years

F orget beaujolais nouveau: a Gloucestershire vineyard has uncorked its 2026 vintage, giving the first taste of this year’s long, hot summer – and an answer to France’s autumn tradition of opening young wine straight after harvest.

Three Choirs near Newent has unveiled its First Release white wine after the earliest harvest in its 50 years of producing wine.

The First Release is what the vineyard calls its “Gloucestershire nouveau” – its tongue-in-cheek nod to beaujolais nouveau, a young, fruity red that is released on the third Thursday in November . Beaujolais nouveau was traditionally made for local consumption and was a way for workers and villages to enjoy the first sip of that year’s harvest.

Vines were first planted on the Gloucestershire site of a fruit farm in 1973, while Three Choirs has been bottling a young wine every November since the 1980s. Customers can buy the wine directly from the vineyard’s shop or try it in its restaurant.

In the 1980s, the harvest used to begin in mid-September, about a month later than it did this year, according to Three Choir’s winemaking director, Martin Fowke.

This year’s prolonged summer of warm temperatures – and rain at the right time – meant the first grapes were picked on 20 August, a week earlier than the previous record set in 2025. The harvest ended on 9 October, by which time 200 tonnes of grapes had been collected across the vineyard’s 30 hectares (74 acres).

The 2026 First Release is a run of 5,000 bottles of a dry, white wine containing solaris, bacchus, siegerrebe and madeleine angevine grapes.

“We now have an extra month to make the wine. We had riper raw material and longer in the winery,” said Fowke, calling 2026 a “record-breaking year”. He added that higher sugar levels and lower acidity allowed winemakers to make a product that was not possible in Britain 30 years ago.

The early timing of the harvest surprised even the Three Choirs winemaker Jack Abbotts, who was on his summer break when picking started. “It’s usually a safe week for me, but this year it all snowballed,” he said.

The changing climate has made it possible to grow grapes on a commercial scale in Britain, but it also brings challenges.

“We found it hard this year,” said Fowke. “People kept saying: ‘This hot weather must be good for you’, but it was difficult because we knew the heat and lack of rain was challenging for farmers. We don’t need it to get any warmer, that’s for sure.”

Vines have been planted as far north as Yorkshire and Scotland , as Britain’s wine industry expands. More than 1,100 vineyards are now registered in Britain.

While Britain remains far down the list of global wine producers in terms of volume – behind countries including Uzbekistan and Tunisia – it is the fastest-growing wine region in the world , according to the property group Knight Frank. The area of planted vineyards in the country has quadrupled since the turn of the century, it reports.

Some of the newer, smaller vineyards do not have their own winemaking facilities, relying on contract winemakers such as Three Choirs. The Gloucestershire vineyard also produces wine for about 40 others, including Llanerch, located west of Cardiff.

English and Welsh wine producers had their second-largest harvest in 2025, when the equivalent of 16.5m bottles, or 124,377 hectolitres, was produced, according to the industry body WineGB.

The data for the 2026 harvest will not be available until early next year, although WineGB said in August it was “optimistic” about the size and quality after the hot growing season.

If the UK climate continues to change and summers such as 2026’s become the norm, Three Choirs may consider growing new varieties. “We can evolve and change, but we would be planting cabernet sauvignon like they did in Bordeaux 50 years ago,” said Fowke, noting the shift from white to red grapes. “But that is not what we set out to do.”

In the fog and damp of November in Gloucestershire, pruning of the vines ready for the 2027 growing season has already begun. “To have two good years in a row is not uncommon, to have three is unusual,” said Fowke.

Wendy Jones, 68, was fatally injured when part of a ceiling collapsed during a bingo game at Pontins Brean Sands

The owner of Pontins holiday parks has been fined £1m over the death of a woman who was fatally injured when part of a ceiling collapsed during a bingo game at a fun park in Somerset .

Eighteen people were injured at the Brean Sands site, near Weston-super-Mare, in February 2019 after ventilation ducting and a 40-metre section of ceiling fell inside an entertainment area known as the Fun Factory.

Wendy Jones, 68, a grandmother from Hereford, was sitting in her mobility scooter for bingo with about 100 others when the ceiling collapsed.

She was among six guests to be treated in hospital after the incident and died six months later. A postmortem examination revealed a clear link between the injuries she suffered and her subsequent death.

Britannia Jinky Jersey, the parent company of Pontins, pleaded guilty at Bristol crown court to failing to discharge its duty to keep the public safe under the Health and Safety at Work Act 1974.

On Friday the company was fined £1m for the offence. Stephen Bennison, 60, an unqualified contractor who had been employed by Britannia Jinky Jersey to install soundproofing in the ceiling, was sentenced to 10 months’ imprisonment, suspended for 18 months.

An investigation by Avon and Somerset police, Somerset council and the Health and Safety Executive found that the ventilation ducting had originally been poorly installed decades earlier, before the site became a Pontins holiday park. But the immediate cause of the collapse was linked to soundproofing work carried out in 2015 when it was under Pontins’ control.

During that work, Bennison stacked heavy sound-insulation slabs on top of the ventilation ducting, the investigation found. It concluded that the insulation in the ceiling appeared to have been leftover material which could not be returned to the supplier – and stacking it on the ducting served no practical purpose.

The court heard that neither Britannia Jinky Jersey Ltd nor Bennison properly assessed whether the ducting could safely bear the significant additional weight.

Rachael Taylor, a specialist prosecutor with the Crown Prosecution Service, said: “A family holiday ended in tragedy because basic safety responsibilities were not met.

“Wendy Jones had every right to expect she was entering a safe environment. Instead, failures by Britannia Jinky Jersey Limited and Stephen Bennison resulted in the collapse of ventilation ducting and the death of a grandmother who was there to play bingo.”

Taylor said Jones’s death was avoidable. She added: “Those responsible for the safety of the public must ensure work is carried out competently and safely. Our thoughts remain with the family and friends of Mrs Jones, and anyone else affected by this tragic incident.”

items.lbText:
Despite the president’s attacks, Sea Services is training New England fishers in offshore wind construction and providing them with a second income stream

O n a rainy September morning, the Pamela Ann, a rusty, 86ft (26-metre) scallop boat, docked in New Bedford, Massachusetts. Its crew had spent the past 12 days at sea, recording mammal sightings, monitoring vessels to ensure they didn’t enter construction zones, and keeping watch over workers at Revolution Wind, a 65-turbine offshore wind project just south of Rhode Island.

“God forbid, if anybody was to fall, we could be there to help them out,” said Capt Kevin Souza, who has a bulldog tattoo on his shin to mark his time in the navy.

Souza and his three-man crew were fishers by trade, but this trip was different. Instead of fishing, they were working for Sea Services North America, a co-op funded through contracts with offshore wind developers.

It was welcome work for these fishers who weather a legally restricted scalloping season. Sea Services retrained the fishers to work in offshore wind and gave them a second stream of income. But this work put them at odds with other fishers who viewed offshore wind as an existential threat to their industry.

Commercial fishers have sued wind companies, arguing that the projects could displace them from their traditional fishing zones and wreak havoc on marine ecosystems (US fishers are allowed to fish in wind-lease zones , except for 500-metre exclusion zones around construction sites, and construction can have positive and negative effects on marine life).

Yet, now, in New England, a cooperative of about 200 fishers is challenging the idea that offshore wind and the fishing industry are natural opponents. Sea Services North America trains and equips fishers to support offshore wind construction, an opportunity that provides them with a second stream of income.

Sea Services pays each fishing boat $4,500 a day plus fuel. Souza, who was initially skeptical of offshore wind, says the opportunity has been a “godsend”.

That godsend, however, may soon come to an end. Since returning to office last year, Donald Trump has systematically attacked offshore wind projects, saying his goal is to not allow any “windmills” to be built. In January 2025, the president issued an executive order halting construction of five offshore wind projects on the east coast.

Sea Services North America was founded in 2020 by another once skeptical fisher. Gary Yerman, 76, had been fishing for more than four decades when he began hearing about proposed commercial-scale offshore wind projects. He and other fishers feared the windfarms could harm their industry. He didn’t want windfarms in his fishing zone, but he believed they were too big to fail. “They’re gonna win,” he thought, deciding to cast his lot with the projects.

In 2019 he and Gordon Videll, a friend and local lawyer, visited Northern Ireland, where they met with fishers who were working with developers building offshore windfarms and other structures. “We saw how it was benefiting the fishermen there,” Yerman said.

Videll noticed that the local fishers drove nice cars. “This provided a real annual income, which, if you’re raising a family, it means everything,” he said.

They returned to the US eager to find a way to bring similar benefits to their fellow fishers – which meant earning the trust of a skeptical industry.

“There was a lot of fellas that were very angry because we joined in on building these windfarms,” said Videll, Sea Services’ CEO. “Nobody trusted it.”

They convinced just one fisher to give it a shot, and over time, more joined.

The pandemic, which struck just as Sea Services was getting off the ground, may have helped Yerman and Videll’s recruitment efforts. As restaurants closed , demand for seafood fell, meaning fishers in New Bedford and nearby fishing towns were looking for extra work. “People had to make decisions they might not have made otherwise,” Videll said.

They found a relatively eager labor pool in local scallopers, who work on boats that are legally restricted from fishing more than 36 days a year to prevent overfishing, leaving the owners of these highly specialized boats looking for extra sources of income during the off-season, said Capt Jack Morris, who owns a fleet of scallop boats including the Pamela Ann, and joined Sea Services in 2021.

“It’s a huge benefit Sea Services has brought,” Morris said. “With the [scallop] fishing season being so short, they are able to continue buying groceries, paying insurance, taking care of the house.”

Stacy Alexander-Nevells, a business owner who works with Sea Services, runs a 19-boat commercial fishing operation with her father. Their boats mostly harvested scallops, but revenues were inconsistent and federal restrictions were always changing. “Working with Sea Services was another income stream,” she said. “We had to diversify. Now the boats aren’t just sitting at the dock, and the guys aren’t unemployed.”

At first, Souza was on the fence about working in offshore wind because most fishers perceived it as working for the enemy, but two decades of scalloping had taken a toll on him. Shucking scallops at a commercial pace eventually causes arthritis, carpal tunnel and rotator cuff tears. Souza lost the tip of a finger, and said he probably has arthritis. “I saw the writing on the wall that scalloping is more of a young man’s game than us older guys,” Souza said.

To date, Sea Services says it has paid vessel owners and fishers a total of $34m for their work at several commercial-scale windfarms. And those benefits have extended to the broader community, Morris said.

“These boats just tie up after their 36 days, but with the windfarm work, they keep going,” Morris said. That means more work for onshore businesses like mechanics, welders, carpenters, electricians and painters, he said.…

items.title: An entrepreneur fights for workers’ protections after his mom was fired after being assaulted at her Saks Fifth Avenue job
items.author: Victoria Bekiempis in New York
items.content:
Jeff Vinokur is using his newly minted wealth from the sale of his edtech company to hold the retail store accountable

Late in the afternoon of 28 June, Jeff Vinokur received a call from his mother that sent him running. “I was assaulted,” Vinokur, a popular science educator known as the “Dancing Scientist”, recalled his mother saying.

Vinokur’s mother, Laza Susuni, was working in the women’s ready-to-wear section at Manhattan’s Saks Fifth Avenue that day when a client attacked her in the dressing room. A court document reviewed by the Guardian corroborates that a woman was arrested at that location on assault and harassment charges.

items.lbText:
Jeff Vinokur is using his newly minted wealth from the sale of his edtech company to hold the retail store accountable

L ate in the afternoon of 28 June, Jeff Vinokur received a call from his mother that sent him running. “I was assaulted,” Vinokur, a popular science educator known as the “ Dancing Scientist ”, recalled his mother saying.

Vinokur’s mother, Laza Susuni, was working in the women’s ready-to-wear section at Manhattan’s Saks Fifth Avenue that day when a client attacked her in the dressing room. A court document reviewed by the Guardian corroborates that a woman was arrested at that location on assault and harassment charges.

Vinokur, 36, who was in New York City visiting Susuni, bounded out of bed, threw on clothes and rushed to the famed department store – not even taking a moment to brush his teeth. Susuni, who said she was kicked in the stomach, was evaluated at a hospital.

While Susuni, 62, was discharged from the hospital later that day without permanent physical injuries, she reeled from panic.

“I could not sleep at all,” said Susuni, who came to the US from Russia as a teen. “I was just so afraid that … she would just come back [to] hurt me, to punish me, and just send somebody to stab me because they put her in handcuffs in front of her own children.”

Susuni said she asked Saks for five days off to recover from her anxiety. She claims that the company instead terminated her.

Vinokur sprang into action, contacting lawyers because he believed that surely such a firing would be illegal. When an attorney said there wasn’t anything he could do, Vinokur thought: “This guy is an idiot, this cannot be, let’s go talk to other lawyers.”

They spoke with about 10 attorneys. “They all say the same thing: that there is no law that protects [against] this,” Vinokur said.

Now Vinokur is taking it upon himself to push for change in New York law to provide broader legal protections for workers against firing if they have been the victims of violent crime on or off the job.

While an employer almost certainly would not tell an employee they were fired for being a crime victim, a workplace might effectively do so by taking issue with things like time off or medical requests, or make spurious claims about lapsed job performance in the wake of the crime.

Alice Jump, a partner at the Reavis Page Jump law firm, said “it doesn’t seem rational” for an employer to behave in such a way, but imagines they might use “taking a lot of time off, or being distressed or emotionally or physically compromised”, as an excuse to terminate a crime victim.

While there are some laws on the books in New York state and city that protect workers from firing in relation to being crime victims, there are limitations. New York state human rights law bars employers from discriminating against, or firing, people because they are victims of domestic violence.

New York state law also prohibits employers from penalizing or firing crime victims for taking time off to appear in court or meet with prosecutors, so long as they give notice of the absence. New York City law makes it illegal for an employee to be fired because they are a victim of domestic violence, sexual assault or stalking, said Jump.

“So if it’s a non-sexual assault, then you’re not specifically covered,” Jump said. “The law doesn’t extend to all crime victims.”

For Jump, it seems that amending legal protections to shield employees who suffer other assaults or violent physical attacks wouldn’t be difficult. “Any kind of assault or violent physical act – you shouldn’t be fired because you’re a subject of that.”

There is no federal law providing termination protections for crime victims, Jump also said.

As part of Vinokur’s campaign for change, he launched a website, Saksfiles.com , outlining not only his mother’s situation but several other alleged instances at Saks stores where former employees have claimed they were fired in relation to being purportedly victimized.

Vinokur, who holds a PhD in biochemistry from UCLA, is also using the media savvy that propelled him from quirky science educator to edtech founder – and vast resources following the sale of his company – to launch an ongoing, in-person protest against Saks.

From 12 November, Vinokur is paying anywhere from more than one to several dozen people to stand outside Saks every day toting signs with text such as “MY MOM IS THE 7th VICTIM. BEATEN AT SAKS. THEN FIRED. I WANT ANSWERS.” Vinokur said that he will pay them to hold signs outside Saks every single day from 1 to 7pm throughout the holiday shopping season – and potentially indefinitely.

“There’s a power element of this – a billion-dollar corporation, the disposable minimum wage worker who is my mom,” Vinokur said. “To me, it’s like: wait a second, I have power now.

“I have this $100m startup exit. I was majority shareholder,” he said. “I don’t have a boat. I don’t fly private. It’s not my style – but I can hold them accountable in a way that I think maybe nobody else can.

“It’s a paid protest. We’re owning it,” he continued. “It’s a very unusual way to go about it, and that’s because I thought: well, if we just go hold signs for a day, nobody cares.”

Vinokur didn’t originally set out to change the system. He wanted Saks to be held accountable. “It was the realization that they got away with this, that they did this to my mom, and they got away with this because there’s no law against it.”

When they couldn’t take legal action, Vinokur then set his sights on the possibility of protest – maybe signs that said “My mom was beaten here and fired.” He then started thinking through the plan “as a scientist” – would anyone care about a beating? “It’s shocking, but that’s not crazy.”

Vinokur started doing research to see whether anything similar had happened at a Saks store. An internet search yielded another example, so Vinokur deployed AI to further research other allegations of crime-related termination and found more.…

items.title: Household rush to stockpile emergency supplies sends British retail sales soaring
items.author: Mark Sweney
items.content:
Surge fuelled by ‘preppers’ heeding Be Ready campaign’s call for households to have three days of food and water for emergencies

The Office for National Statistics (ONS) said the volume of goods sold jumped by 0.7% month on month in October, defying economists’ consensus expectations of flat sales, as “preppers” took heed of the government’s Be Ready campaign to hold supplies to last 72 hours to survive a possible extreme weather event, cyber incident or another serious emergency.

items.lbText:
Surge fuelled by ‘preppers’ heeding Be Ready campaign’s call for households to have three days of food and water for emergencies

Retail sales in Great Britain surged last month as the public rushed to buy products including tinned food and long-life milk, after the government issued a warning to stock up in case of a disaster.

The Office for National Statistics (ONS) said that the volume of goods sold jumped by 0.7% month-on month in October, defying economists’ consensus expectations of flat sales, as “preppers” took heed of the government’s Be Ready campaign to hold supplies to last 72 hours to survive a possible extreme weather event, cyber incident or another serious emergency.

The surge in sales is a welcome bounce back for the industry after a poor September , which the ONS has revised down from a 0.4% fall to a 0.6% fall, fuelled in part by poor online sales of autumn and winter clothing because of unseasonably warm weather.

“Supermarkets have told us that sales of long-life food items such as tinned food and UHT milk were boosted by the government’s ‘Be Ready’ campaign,” said Grant Fitzner, chief economist at the ONS.

Food store sales, primarily supermarkets, rose by 0.8% month-on-month, the fastest rate since the 1.4% rise in April.

Textile, clothing and footwear stores reported a 1.5% month-on-month boost. An increase in visits to galleries, and a jump in sales of sports equipment, games and toys, lifted sales across other non-food stores by 3.1% month-on-month, the biggest rise since January.

The total non-food stores category – which includes department stores, clothing, household and other non-food stores – increased by 1.1% month-on-month in October.

Non-store retail sales, primarily online but also sellers such as street stalls and markets, bounced back too, rising 0.9% as a turn in the weather last month drove sales of autumn and winter ranges.

However, sales volumes of motor fuel fell by 2.2% last month, the steepest rate since April, as prices at the pump rose.

“October’s retail sales have exceeded expectations, despite low consumer confidence and growing pressure on household finances from higher interest rates and inflation,” said Erin Brookes, European retail and consumer lead at Alvarez & Marsal.

“Retailers will be feeling optimistic as the sector approaches the critical Black Friday and Christmas trading period, with October’s sales growth suggesting consumers are still willing to spend this festive season.

“Despite this positivity, retailers are caught between increasingly price-sensitive consumers and mounting operating costs.”

items.title: Don’t blame cyber-attacks for recent outages. The real villain is the US economy | Bruce Schneier
items.author: Bruce Schneier
items.content:
Our tech infrastructure is riddled with problems. But they’re all downstream of the incentives baked into shareholder capitalism

It’s been a bad week for our computerized infrastructure. We’ve seen outages at Microsoft, the FAA, a handful of banks, United Airlines, an unnamed classified NSA network, and Apple. People should be forgiven for suspecting a coordinated cyber-attack, a common cause, or at least a conspiracy. But there is none.

The incidents are unrelated. They’re not the result of any cyber-attack, coordinated or not. And, even more surprising, they don’t seem to be the result of AI. (We can’t say anything about the NSA; we’ll probably never know the details of that one.) It’s really just a series of unfortunate coincidences.

Continue reading...
items.lbText:
Our tech infrastructure is riddled with problems. But they’re all downstream of the incentives baked into shareholder capitalism

I t’s been a bad week for our computerized infrastructure. We’ve seen outages at Microsoft , the FAA , a handful of banks , United Airlines , an unnamed classified NSA network , and Apple . People should be forgiven for suspecting a coordinated cyber-attack, a common cause, or at least a conspiracy. But there is none.

The incidents are unrelated. They’re not the result of any cyber-attack, coordinated or not. And, even more surprising, they don’t seem to be the result of AI. (We can’t say anything about the NSA; we’ll probably never know the details of that one.) It’s really just a series of unfortunate coincidences.

None of them should surprise, though. Our computerized infrastructure is both vulnerable and fragile.

Much of it is old and has been incrementally patched and upgraded over the decades. A surprising amount of it is maintained by hobbyists, without any recompense. There often aren’t good backup systems. And more and more of it is centralized, meaning that individual failures have cascading consequences across many different aspects of our lives and society.

A lot of our tech infrastructure just barely works. And when it fails, it can fail badly. It’s the very opposite of resilience.

There are a lot of technological reasons why this is true, but they are all downstream from the economic ones. The technologies we rely on are built and maintained within our economic system – and that’s where the core problems lie.

Security, safety, resilience, redundancy and recoverability are all essential parts of reliable technology, but they are all costs. More importantly, they are costs that don’t generate near-term profits.

Modern shareholder capitalism, and private equity in particular, prioritizes near-term profits over everything else. This squeezes all apparent inefficiencies – and, additionally, all other positive intangibles – out of a company in pursuit of those profits.

Market competition, essential for the forces that nudge companies to provide better services, is another perceived inefficiency. Monopolization removes it in pursuit of near-term profits.

From the perspective of a quarterly budget, spending on reliability measures is an inefficiency. They’re expenses that don’t generate revenue. They feel wasteful … until something bad happens.

But, if you’re lucky, you can push the costs of failure on to society, further increasing profits. So, we get stranded in airports when planes don’t fly, or have to deal with the fallout when we can’t withdraw money from our bank accounts.

The effects of those economic pressures are brittle systems, with single points of failure and cascading failure modes. They’re more susceptible to cyber-attack – both human and AI-fueled – and more susceptible to random mistakes.

The more we allow unregulated capitalism to privatize gains while socializing risks, the more we should expect these sorts of failures.

Upgrading our computerized systems, increasing their reliability, removing single points of failure, and making them more resilient are all technical problems. But they won’t happen until we fix the political and economic ones.

We need to change the economic incentives that make it profitable to operate these systems just at the edge of functionality, and to push the costs of failure on to all of us. Fixing that requires regulation – with enforcement and meaningful fines – and stringent antitrust enforcement.

But while that’s all easy to say, it’s much harder to implement – especially in the US where monied interests have such a tight hold on the legislative agenda. Until this changes, we should expect lots more of these sorts of failures in the future.

Bruce Schneier is a security technologist who teaches at the Harvard Kennedy School at Harvard University and the University of Toronto’s Munk School

items.title: AI is imposing a hidden ‘cognitive tax’ on the lowest-paid workers
items.author: Henrietta Moore
items.content:
It’s time to rethink welfare as AI reshapes the economy and wears down the brains of some of the most vulnerable workers

AI is adding to the cognitive load of workers already stretched thin by unpredictable pay, insecure housing and mounting debt – and the lowest paid feel it most. We need to rethink welfare for an economy being reshaped by AI.

Throughout the history of the study of economics, the human brain, which directs our labour, judgment and resilience, has rarely been considered an asset in its own right. The emerging AI economy is changing that. As machines take on routine work, what becomes most valuable is the judgment, creativity and insights only people can provide. Economists coined a term for this in recent years: brain capital.

Professor Dame Henrietta Moore is founder and director of the UCL Institute for Global Prosperity and co-leads The New Alignment, the institute’s G20 policy programme

It’s time to rethink welfare as AI reshapes the economy and wears down the brains of some of the most vulnerable workers

A I is adding to the cognitive load of workers already stretched thin by unpredictable pay, insecure housing and mounting debt – and the lowest paid feel it most. We need to rethink welfare for an economy being reshaped by AI.

Throughout the history of the study of economics, the human brain, which directs our labour, judgment and resilience, has rarely been considered an asset in its own right. The emerging AI economy is changing that. As machines take on routine work, what becomes most valuable is the judgment, creativity and insights only people can provide. Economists coined a term for this in recent years: brain capital.

The World Economic Forum finds analytical thinking is now the skill employers value most, and estimates that 59 in every 100 workers will need training to adapt to this shift by 2030.

In September, I found myself at the first Global Brain Economy Summit in New York asking a hard question: how much room is there for creativity and learning when one’s mind is consumed by anxieties about paying rent or for food to last through the week?

There are two new indices that rank countries and US states on brain capital, using about 60 indicators ranging from child poverty to the prevalence of Parkinson’s disease. Yet they both possess a flaw: neither measures whether people’s livelihoods are secure – whether income is predictable, debts are manageable or homes are safe. The World Health Organization counts safety and security among the foundations of brain health, but nobody building these indices asked people what drains their mental capacity.

I call this missing liability “cognitive taxation”. It is a tax no government voted for, levied on attention, memory and the capacity to learn, and collected through rents, debts and welfare paperwork. Worry over insecurity runs in the background like an app draining a phone battery, and over years, the chronic stress wears down the brain itself. And AI is raising the rate.

Livelihood pressures stack up to exceed what one mind can handle. Poverty manufactures its own interest payments. Imagine a week in which a worker’s rent goes up and she loses a shift at the last minute, something common for workers without guaranteed hours. She puts the shortfall on a credit card. Preoccupied with finding the rent, she returns a benefits form late and loses part of her benefits payment as a penalty. Three small setbacks leave her household poorer in money, headspace and health.

Financial scarcity measurably impairs how well people think, but the effect lifts when the pressure does too, according to a 2024 analysis of 112,000 people in the Journal of Economic Psychology. Low-paid workers in rural India who received their wages a few days early were 7% more productive and made fewer mistakes. When South Africa lowered the pension age for men from 65 to 60, those who became eligible earlier showed slower memory decline and were about five percentage points less likely to develop dementia.

Though AI is increasing the value of human judgment, it also increases cognitive taxation. Automation makes work less predictable, shifting and shortening schedules, long before it eliminates jobs, as Walmart staff dealing with AI-set schedules have found. Meanwhile, overseeing AI tools also adds mental fatigue, according to research by the Boston Consulting Group. Workers required to retrain for the AI economy will struggle to learn new skills if their minds are already occupied by worries over pay, housing and debt.

Britain shows what insecurity already costs before AI adds to it. About 2.7 million people there are out of work through long-term sickness. And my institute’s research found that people facing insecurity across several areas of life carry an earnings penalty as large as the gender pay gap, one that roughly doubles after seven years. Those findings suggest that worry erodes how well people work. Now the UK’s AI minister says the government must seriously consider that the tech could have “ an unprecedented impact ” on the jobs market. Worries abound and compound.

When Elon Musk told reporters at the White House in September that AI would bring “universal high income”, he offered Silicon Valley’s favourite answer to job losses: cash. Yet a study funded by Sam Altman, giving low-income Americans $1,000 a month, found that mental health gains faded after the first year. Extra cash helps, but it cannot guarantee a place for your child at a nursery or a bus that gets you to work on time. These pressures already tax the minds of people in work, and no payment removes them.

The better answer to cognitive tax and job loss is universal basic services, providing childcare, housing, transport and digital access, free at the point of use. The principle is the one behind the UK’s National Health Service: people should be able to rely on essential support without facing a bill when they use it. Extending free childcare alone is expected to bring 60,000 non-working parents into jobs in the UK.

Every government should ask this question of every fiscal policy: how will this policy affect the cognitive load of the poorest people it touches? Britain, which takes over the G20 presidency after December’s summit in Miami, should put it to the world’s largest economies. This question belongs in every treasury’s fiscal plans, brain-capital indices and AI-powered public services before they launch.

Sixty years ago we learned to count the damage economies do to the air and water, and it has changed how we build infrastructure for the better. Now that AI is making our minds the most valuable thing we have, it is time we count the damage done to them.

Professor Dame Henrietta Moore is founder and director of the UCL Institute for Global Prosperity and co-leads The New Alignment, the institute’s G20 policy programme
